This person is a 64-year-old warehouse picker in Laredo, Texas, with 41 years on the job and chronic back pain, who argues the age increase should include an arduous work carve-out based on objective physical-demand scores (such as O*NET), grandfather anyone within five years of retirement, allow full benefits at 66 for verified hazardous or manual careers, and expand early-claim penalty waivers for low-wage lifetime contributors. After a slipped disc last year forced me to miss six weeks and cut back to shorter shifts, I know I can't physically make it to 68 without an arduous-work carve-out. Because I’m 64 and within five years of the current age, a grandfather clause would let me retire at 66, but without it I’d either have to grind out two more years or accept a steep early-claim cut. Because O*NET scores warehouse order picking high on strength and manual handling, an objective arduous-work carve-out would let me retire at 66, but without it I’d be forced to risk reinjury on the floor or take a steep early-claim cut. My Social Security statement shows that if the full retirement age moves to 68 and I have to claim at 66, I'd lose about $300 a month—money I need for rent and prescriptions.

This person is a 46-year-old public pension actuary in Washington, DC, who supports a phased increase tied to birth cohorts (for example, two months per quarter starting in 2027), automatic longevity indexing thereafter, an explicit minimum-benefit floor to protect the bottom quartile, and strict, costed criteria with caps for any occupational exceptions to keep the system solvent and predictable. I turn 67 in 2046, so a cohort-based phase-in lets me plan around the change without a sudden two-year cliff while keeping the trust fund on track. After my dad was laid off at 62 and had to claim early, I became adamant about establishing a real minimum-benefit floor for the bottom quartile. As a 1979 cohort, a sudden jump to 68 would force me to boost savings by several thousand dollars a year or work longer, whereas a two-months-per-quarter phase-in keeps my plan intact. From an actuarial standpoint, I’d base the automatic longevity index on cohort life expectancy at 62 with a hard cap of two months per year to prevent volatile swings.

This person is a 62-year-old home health aide in Detroit, a single mother who took unpaid years to care for relatives, who wants caregiver credits of up to five years to count toward eligibility and benefit formulas, a reduced-penalty early option at 64 for high-injury occupations, funded retraining into less physical roles, and strong age-discrimination enforcement so older aides are not pushed out before reaching the new age. If retraining funds let her shift into scheduling or case coordination, she could keep working to 68; without that, her back won’t hold up in the field. At 60, her agency cut her hours saying they needed “younger backs,” which is why enforcement against age discrimination is non-negotiable for her. If retraining funds pay for a short scheduling/case coordinator certificate at the community college, I can move off heavy lifting and work to 68; without that, I’d need a reduced-penalty early option at 64 to avoid wrecking my back. I took four unpaid years to care for my mother with dementia, and those zeros in my Social Security record will lower my benefit unless caregiver credits replace them.

This person is a 42-year-old payroll software product manager in Silicon Valley who insists on a single federal effective date, machine-readable SSA specifications and test sandboxes, unambiguous cohort rules by birthdate, minimal occupation-based carve-outs in favor of the disability channel, and at least 18 months of lead time so employers can update systems without payroll errors. After we had to issue thousands of corrections from a leap-day birthdate edge case in a state benefit change, I insist SSA publish machine-readable cohort rules with canonical test cases. I lead the team that encodes SSA eligibility into payroll engines for 20,000 employers, so staggered cohorts or carve-outs multiply edge cases and trigger costly correction waves. If Congress phases it in by birth quarter instead of a single national cutover, our support tickets will spike and we’ll burn multiple sprints building 200+ new test cases to avoid another correction wave. If they phase it in by birth quarter or occupation, we'd face a rules explosion and a seven-figure revalidation effort across our 20,000 clients.

This person is a 55-year-old construction union leader in Chicago representing electricians and laborers, who demands a negotiated list of arduous and hazardous trades eligible for earlier full benefits, bridge benefits between ages 62 and 68 funded partly by employers, a mandatory right to transfer to lighter-duty positions after age 60, and protection of multiemployer plan agreements during the transition. After tearing his rotator cuff on a downtown site at 50 and only staying in the trade by shifting to a steward role, he insists any age hike include a guaranteed right to transfer to lighter-duty work after 60. His older brother had to retire at 61 after back surgery and saw his pension cut by nearly a quarter, so he’s adamant about employer-funded bridge benefits and an enforceable right to lighter-duty work after 60. He has filed three grievances this year for members over 60 denied light-duty reassignment, convincing him the transfer right must be enforceable with penalties. His doctor has already restricted him from overhead work, so he wants the law to make light-duty transfers a right, not a favor.

This person is a 38-year-old economist at a nonpartisan think tank in Washington, DC, who favors raising the age to 68 over 12 years, implementing actuarially fair early and late retirement adjustments, aligning public and private retirement ages, expanding SSA disability capacity with faster determinations, and adding a wage subsidy for older low-wage workers to encourage continued work. After watching their mother wait nearly two years for a disability determination in her early 60s, they view boosting SSA capacity and speed as the nonnegotiable piece of any retirement age hike. Seeing her sell her car to pay rent during that wait is why I insist on interim disability payments and a 90-day decision standard before any age hike. At 38, I’d be in the cohort fully affected by any faster phase-in, so clear grandfathering and communication are essential for my own retirement planning. Still paying off grad‑school loans, I’d see my savings window squeezed if the phase‑in is accelerated without robust grandfathering just as childcare costs peak.

This person is a 67-year-old public librarian in rural New Mexico piecing together part-time shifts, who wants a partial-retirement option that allows claiming, for example, 50 percent of benefits at 66 while working without the earnings test cliff, clearer part-time crediting rules, and targeted outreach and digital literacy support so rural seniors can plan the change. At 66 I picked up extra Saturday shifts and then saw part of my Social Security check withheld by the earnings test, which felt like a penalty for keeping our tiny branch open. If the age moves to 68 without a partial-benefit option, I’ll either have to drop the Saturday shifts that keep our branch open or see more of my check clawed back by the earnings test. The nearest SSA office is 90 miles away and our library’s internet is unreliable, so I only figured out the earnings test after my check arrived smaller. The smaller deposit that month triggered a $35 overdraft fee on my account.

This person is a 35-year-old Social Security field office manager in Atlanta who wants simplified hardship criteria to avoid appeals backlogs, budget for additional adjudicators and call center staff during the transition, standardized national forms, automatic cohort notifications mailed 24 months before each change, and a small-scale pilot in two regions before nationwide rollout. During the 2020–21 call surge, we were on mandatory overtime for months, so if the age shifts without extra adjudicators and call-center staff, my office will be overwhelmed again. During the last rule change, our appeals inventory doubled, which is why I insist on a two‑region pilot and 24‑month cohort notices before any age shift. I still field weekly calls from claimants confused by the last age change, which is why standardized national forms and 24‑month cohort notices are nonnegotiable for me. If it's phased by birth cohort with 24-month mailers and updated scripts, my team can absorb it; a single hard effective date would flood our lobby and phones for months.

This person is a 58-year-old firefighter battalion chief in Sacramento nearing eligibility for a public safety pension and a deferred retirement option plan, who argues the implementation must preserve earlier retirement for hazardous service, credit years spent on front-line duty, formalize pathways to administrative roles with continued accruals, and recognize PTSD and cumulative trauma under hardship exemptions. I’m a year from entering my DROP and moving into a training chief post, so if the age rises without crediting my 26 years on suppression and allowing accruals in admin, it upends the pension math I’ve planned for. If there's no grandfather clause for members within a year of DROP, I'd have to delay my transition to training chief and take a sizable hit to my projected pension. I’ve had two PTSD claims denied because they weren’t tied to a single incident, which is why explicit cumulative trauma language in the hardship exemption matters to me. If the bill includes a rule-of-85 (age plus service) for public safety, I’d qualify next year at 59 with 27 years and could enter DROP and take the training chief job as planned.

This person is a 40-year-old state budget director in Sacramento who supports harmonizing retirement ages across state and local plans, limiting exceptions to narrowly defined categories with sunset reviews, requiring that deferred retirement option and early-out programs be actuarially neutral, mandating data reporting on retirements and overtime to prevent cost spikes, and funding a time-limited transition supplement within existing contributions. After a 2018 department early-out triggered a costly overtime surge, I’m laser-focused on tying any age hike to real-time reporting and strict actuarial neutrality. If we don’t harmonize state and local ages, departments will shift staffing to looser plans and blow holes in my five-year forecast. My five-year plan banks savings from uniform ages and neutral DROP/early-outs, so carve-outs would force me to backfill with agency cuts or deferred maintenance. Because I must certify actuarial neutrality to rating agencies, I want the statute to require independent actuarial sign‑off and quarterly overtime/retirement reporting before any DROP or early‑out is offered.

This person is a 64-year-old union construction laborer in Ohio with a 41-year contribution history who insists any increase to 68 include an arduous-occupation carve-out using objective job-exposure and physical-demand criteria and an unreduced early option for 40-plus years of contributions, because his worn joints and peers' shorter life expectancy make a uniform increase inequitable. If there's no grandfathering for near-retirees, I'd have to push past 66 and keep climbing scaffolds on worn knees despite 41 years of contributions. After a rotator cuff tear from hauling rebar sidelined me for eight weeks last summer, my doctor warned me that working past 66 could cause permanent damage. My pension counselor calculated that without an unreduced 40-year option, I’d lose about $350 a month if I retire at 66. If they phase it in and exempt workers within two years of eligibility, I could retire at 66 without penalty and avoid risking permanent shoulder damage.

This person is a 42-year-old public pension actuary in New York who backs raising the age via a transparent longevity index and a two-month-per-birth-cohort phase-in, paired with actuarially neutral early and late claiming factors and a narrowly defined, periodically reviewed hardship list, to keep the system solvent while limiting loopholes. Seeing my uncle forced off a New York bridge crew with a blown shoulder at 61 made me insist the hardship list cover truly wear-and-tear jobs but stay narrowly defined and regularly reviewed. As someone who’ll be paying payroll taxes for two more decades, I care most that early/late claiming factors be truly actuarially neutral so costs aren’t shifted onto my cohort. As someone born in 1983, I’d be squarely in the affected cohorts, so the two-month-per-birth-cohort phase-in is personally important to avoid a sudden two-year cliff. I’ve planned our kids’ college and our mortgage around a gradual two-month step-up, and a sudden two-year jump would blow that timing.

This person is a 58-year-old warehouse picker in Texas with osteoarthritis who wants a pathway to claim partial benefits before 68 with smaller penalties for long-tenure workers, plus funded retraining vouchers if staying employed, because the current cliff between disability and full retirement does not fit her declining capacity. If the age rises to 68 without an early-partial pathway, she'd likely have to leave for disability and lose her employer health plan, whereas long-tenure credits and a retraining voucher could keep her working light duty. Last year I was denied SSDI because I can still lift 20 lbs, but I can’t sustain 10-hour pick rates, so an early-partial option would let me keep my employer insurance and move to light duty. If early-partial benefits recognized years in physically demanding work, my penalty would drop enough that I could cut to 30 hours and keep my health plan while training for inventory control. If retraining vouchers covered a community college inventory software certificate, I could shift to light duty within a year instead of filing for disability.

This person is a 38-year-old logistics HR director in Illinois who supports a higher retirement age but only alongside employer tax credits for ergonomic upgrades, federal standards for phased retirement allowing part-time work while drawing partial benefits, and clearer disability adjudication to deter gaming and keep older staff productive. Last year we cut musculoskeletal claims by about a third after investing in lift‑assist pallet jacks and height-adjustable pack stations, so I’m adamant any age increase be paired with ergonomic tax credits so smaller depots can afford the same upgrades. The ergonomic credit needs to be refundable and cover retrofits and leased equipment—like lift‑assist add‑ons and height‑adjustable stations—because many of our smaller depots lease space and can’t finance big capital buys. When a 62-year-old picker asked to go part-time after a back injury, the lack of clear phased-retirement rules forced an all-or-nothing choice and we lost him—so that provision is non-negotiable for me. I’ve already drafted a phased‑retirement program with 25–30 hour shifts and prorated benefits, but I can’t roll it out until there’s clear federal guidance on drawing partial Social Security while working.

This person is a 60-year-old Latina home health aide in California who paused work to care for her mother and argues the reform must add caregiving credits and count documented caregiving years toward a service-based early retirement threshold, with a minimum benefit floor so interrupted careers are not punished. After taking two unpaid years off to care for my mother after her stroke, I saw my Social Security estimate drop, so without caregiving credits and a minimum benefit floor I’d be penalized for that time. If the reform includes up to two years of caregiving credits, I could still retire at 66; without them, I'd be forced to keep doing heavy shifts until 68. If caregiving credits are capped at one year, I’d still miss the service-based threshold and be stuck doing heavy overnight shifts to make up the difference. I have no employer pension and little savings, so the minimum benefit floor is what keeps me from falling into poverty if my caregiving years aren’t credited.

This person is a 47-year-old tax policy analyst at a nonpartisan D.C. think tank who favors implementing the age hike with a points system combining age and years of covered earnings so long-tenured, lower-wage workers can retire before 68, offset by slightly higher early-claim penalties and enhanced delayed credits to keep it revenue neutral. Watching my father retire early from a physically demanding warehouse job after nearly 40 years of contributions makes me insist the points formula protect long-tenured, lower-wage workers. In our microsimulations, a 95-point cutoff (age plus years of covered earnings) paired with a 0.3% higher early-claim penalty keeps the reform revenue neutral while preserving earlier eligibility for 35–40-year workers. Since a pure age hike would delay my own full retirement age to 68, I insist on a points path that still lets long-tenured workers claim earlier. After weeks helping my dad appeal a denied SSDI claim when his back gave out, I became adamant that a clear points path should spare worn‑down workers from being forced onto disability.

This person is a 66-year-old firefighter in Massachusetts who contends public safety and other hazardous-duty roles should keep separate, lower retirement ages based on occupational mortality data, and that anyone within five years of eligibility be fully grandfathered to prevent mid-career goalpost shifts. I'm set to retire at 66 this year, and without a strong grandfather clause I'd have to stay on the line two more years despite a torn rotator cuff and smoke-related lung damage from a 2018 mill fire. I've already put off shoulder surgery until after my planned retirement because I can't afford months off the line, and raising the age now would force me to keep working injured. Under Massachusetts Group 4 rules I’m already at the 80% pension cap after 32 years, so raising the age to 68 wouldn’t increase my benefit but would delay my surgery and risk permanent damage. If the increase were limited to new hires or those more than five years out, it wouldn’t touch me. An immediate across-the-board bump would keep me on the line injured for two more years with no added pension.

This person is a 33-year-old municipal budget officer in Michigan who wants the age raised for general employees with automatic future adjustments tied to life expectancy and plan funding ratios, limited grandfathering to manage costs, and clear occupation definitions to prevent creep into the hazardous tier. Last year I had to cut weekend library hours to cover a sudden pension contribution spike, so I want formula-based age adjustments with minimal grandfathering. During the last bargaining cycle I had to push back on three departments trying to reclassify admin roles as "hazardous," which is why I want a tight statutory definition. My city's latest MERS valuation spiked our employer contribution rate by 3.7 percentage points midyear, so I want an automatic age trigger that kicks in when the funded ratio drops below 80% or when mortality tables are updated. As the person building our five-year budget, I need trigger decisions tied to the MERS annual valuation with a one-year lead time to avoid midyear cuts.

This person is a 25-year-old gig economy driver and community college student in Arizona who supports moving to 68 if it is coupled with mandatory platform contributions to Social Security, stronger age-discrimination enforcement, and portable, phased-retirement options so today's nontraditional workers actually reach the new age with adequate credits. I’ve already missed a Social Security credit because my app earnings are inconsistent across platforms, so mandatory per‑trip contributions matter most to me. Because Phoenix summers force me to cut back driving, I need per‑trip minimum contributions so those weeks still accrue toward a quarterly credit. I especially want cross‑app aggregation so my Uber, Lyft, and DoorDash trips count together toward each quarterly credit. I’ve watched older drivers in my Phoenix rideshare group get deactivated after minor complaints, so stronger age‑bias enforcement is essential if we’re expected to work until 68.

This person is a 54-year-old Social Security Administration regional operations manager in Georgia who stresses the need for a simple birth-year schedule, a national outreach campaign and better calculators to cut claiming errors, temporary hiring of disability adjudicators to handle spillover, and a short, well-documented hardship exemption to keep administration feasible. After the 2015 file-and-suspend changes, my region spent months correcting misfiled claims and fielding appeals, so I'm adamant we pair any age shift with a simple birth-year schedule and upgraded calculators. If it’s phased in monthly instead of by birth-year cohorts, I’ll be the one authorizing overtime and retraining front-line staff to fix the inevitable wave of misfiled claims. I'm 54, so a monthly phase-in would muddle my own retirement timing while I’m managing everyone else’s. If the hardship exemption isn’t narrowly defined with a short, checklist-based documentation standard, my region will face inconsistent decisions and years of appeals.

This person is a 64-year-old scaffolder in a post-industrial town who has done heavy outdoor work since his teens; he supports exemptions for physically demanding occupations, wants grandfathering for those within five years of retirement, and argues for an early-access option at 66 with predictable actuarial reductions because his life expectancy and injury history make two more years unrealistic. After a fall on site last year that tore his rotator cuff, his GP warned he shouldn’t be working at height beyond 65. Since the fall he’s been on reduced hours doing ground work, so without a five-year grandfather clause he’d face a two-year income gap his modest savings can’t cover. I’ve paid National Insurance since I was 16 and already have 48 qualifying years, so pushing my State Pension age to 68 without a five-year grandfather clause feels like moving the goalposts for those of us who started young. I'd support a long-contributions rule so anyone with 45+ years of NI, like me, can still claim at 66 even if the State Pension age rises to 68.

This person is a 38-year-old government actuary in the national treasury who models pension solvency; she favors raising the age via an automatic index to life expectancy, phasing it in by birth cohort over eight years to avoid cliffs, and tightening early-retirement pathways to protect the fund and provide a transparent schedule for households and markets. After seeing a previous one-off change spur a rush of early-retirement claims that destabilized her projections, she now prioritizes pairing an indexed age with tighter early-exit rules. Because her solvency projections feed directly into debt issuance schedules and credit-rating briefings, she prioritizes an automatic index that minimizes policy surprises and behavioral shocks. She still recalls fielding urgent calls from ratings analysts when a previous cliff change blew a hole in her solvency projections. She wants the index to use a rolling five-year life expectancy average with a 0.25-year annual cap so her solvency path stays predictable.

This person is a 67-year-old low-wage supermarket cashier in a coastal city with arthritis and limited savings; she wants a partial-retirement design that lets her draw 50% of her pension while working up to 20 hours without punitive earnings tests, plus funded workplace accommodations and enforcement against age discrimination so she can bridge to full retirement safely. After being reprimanded for using a stool during an arthritis flare, she knows enforceable accommodations and anti-retaliation rules are as crucial as a 20-hour, no-penalty partial pension. Because hurricane closures make her hours spike and dip, she wants any earnings threshold averaged monthly so a couple of busy weeks won’t wipe out her 50% partial pension. After last year’s hurricane, she worked ten straight days to restock and realized a strict weekly earnings cap would strip her 50% benefit in the very weeks she most needed it. Without those protections, she fears she’d have to claim early and lock in a permanent benefit cut because her arthritis no longer lets her manage full-time shifts.

This person is a 49-year-old human resources director at a regional logistics firm in a suburban corridor; he supports a higher age if paired with employer tax credits for reskilling workers 55+, clear accommodation guidelines, and a published phase-in calendar so he can plan staffing, avoid a pre-change retirement wave, and budget for older workers' benefits. When a 2019 pension tweak sparked an early-retirement surge that left him short 12 CDL drivers and 3 dispatchers for months, he became adamant about a published, phased timeline to avoid another cliff. He especially wants the reskilling credit to be refundable and payable quarterly so he can cash-flow CDL refresher and dispatch software training for employees 55+. If the reskilling credit isn’t refundable and paid quarterly, his Q3 cash crunch would force him to defer CDL refresher and dispatch software training for 55+ staff, increasing turnover risk right before peak season. After spending about $180,000 on overtime and spot-market carriers to cover the 2019 early-retirement gap, he now views a 24–36 month phased timeline as nonnegotiable.

This person is a 60-year-old rural caregiver who left paid work to care for a spouse with dementia; she opposes a blanket increase unless it includes credited years for unpaid caregiving, a compassionate early-access route with a means test, and the ability to combine a carer allowance with partial pension payments to prevent poverty. I left my job at 57 when my husband's dementia advanced, so without caregiving credits or early access a rise to 68 would leave a two-year income gap we can't bridge. Because the nearest respite center is 45 miles away and costs more than I could earn locally, being allowed to combine a carer allowance with a partial pension is what would actually keep us afloat. If each year I provide 35+ hours of unpaid care counted as a full pension credit, I could accept the higher retirement age. After the council scrapped our respite grant last year, I burned through our savings on petrol and day‑centre fees, so even a short gap in pension access would push us into arrears.

This person is a 35-year-old startup founder and high-earning taxpayer in a tech hub; he backs raising the age with a firm timetable, prefers progressive benefit formulas or means testing to protect low earners, and wants automatic enrollment into supplemental savings so younger cohorts are not hit with higher payroll taxes. As an employer scaling headcount, I’d rather implement automatic 401(k) auto-enrollment with default escalation than absorb a payroll tax hike that would raise our burn and slow hiring. On our current $20M payroll, a 1% hike would add about $200,000 a year to burn—roughly the cost of one senior engineer we wouldn’t be able to hire. I’m even willing to see my own future benefit reduced by means-testing if it keeps FICA rates flat and the age increase is phased in over a clear 10-year schedule. After piloting 401(k) auto-enrollment at a 6% default with 1% annual escalation, our participation rose from 58% to 94% without raising cash comp, cementing my preference over a FICA increase.

This person is a 52-year-old urban teachers' union policy lead who negotiates pension terms; she argues against a one-size-fits-all change, pushing instead for sector-specific rules that credit years of service, optional buyouts for near-retirees, and carve-outs for high-burnout roles to maintain recruitment and morale. Having spent 27 years in the classroom before moving into union work, her own retirement plan relies on counting years of service toward full benefits so she isn’t forced to work to 68. Because my plan relies on a Rule-of-85 service credit, I’m set to retire with full benefits at 60; switching to a hard age-68 minimum would erase that and delay my retirement by eight years. I’ve already purchased two years of service credit to qualify under Rule‑of‑85 at 60, so without a grandfather clause that investment is wasted and I’m forced to work until 68. In our last contract I bargained smaller raises to preserve our Rule‑of‑85, so moving to a hard 68 now would move the goalposts on a tradeoff I—and my members—already paid for.

This person is a 50-year-old municipal budget director in a fiscally stressed city; he wants a uniform national retirement age, coordinated across public and private plans, limited early-retirement windows to prevent staffing gaps, and temporary retention bonuses funded by savings to manage the transition without service disruptions. Last year, a rush of firefighters retiring before a policy change forced us to spend $4.2M on overtime, so a coordinated national phase-in with retention bonuses is critical. Our actuary shows that unsynchronized early-retirement spikes add roughly 0.2% to our annual required pension contribution, so I prioritize a uniform national phase-in with capped early windows. As the official who must certify a balanced budget each quarter, I’ve modeled that a uniform 24–36 month phase-in with capped three-month early-out windows and a 2% retention bonus keeps our five-year plan balanced by year two. If the federal change isn’t synchronized across Social Security, state pension statutes, and 457 plans with the same effective date, we’ll be stuck running dual eligibility and benefit projections for up to two years—a six-figure administrative hit I can’t absorb.

This person is a 46-year-old disability rights attorney at a legal aid clinic who represents workers with chronic conditions; she insists the policy include clear incapacity carve-outs with standardized functional assessments, fast-track appeals, and interim benefits during adjudication so genuinely unfit workers are not forced into hardship. She watched a client with lupus lose housing while waiting nine months for a decision, so she prioritizes guaranteed interim benefits and a 45-day fast-track appeal. After her clinic nearly ran out of emergency funds during a surge of denied claims last year, she insists interim benefits be automatic within 14 days of filing. Her own sister, a home health aide with rheumatoid arthritis, nearly lost custody during a months-long benefits limbo, making fast-track appeals nonnegotiable for her. She insists the standardized functional assessments explicitly account for fatigue, cognitive fog, and flare variability—not just lab values—so autoimmune and chronic pain clients aren’t wrongly denied.

This person is a 55-year-old senior compliance auditor at the national pension agency who designs anti-fraud controls; he supports raising the age only if paired with robust verification for disability and hardship exemptions, data matching with health records, randomized audits, and adequate staffing and IT to implement changes without backlogs or abuse. He led a 2021 pilot linking claims to national health records that cut fraudulent approvals by 18%, convincing him that data integration and randomized audits must precede any age hike. After the 2018 backlog left him triaging fraud flags while genuine hardship claims sat for months, he’s adamant the system be fortified before any age hike. He would be tasked with rolling out the tougher exemption checks, so he wants the bill to earmark funding and require SLAs for health-record APIs before the age increase takes effect. At 55, a blanket increase would delay his own retirement by two years, so he wants the age change contingent on meeting staffing targets and health‑record API SLAs.
